catalog_quote: [p. 55] There are two tones in Ikaan, a high tone (H) and a low tone (L). After floating L, H is downstepped. As all following chapters in this thesis are concerned with tone, no further information will be given here. [p. 56] Possible syllable structures in Ikaan are V, CV and CVC. In all three types, V can be either long or short. ... The minimal word in Ikaan is bimoraic. Since most Ikaan words consist of a root prefixed with a vowel they automatically have two moras. [p. 339] Ikaan of course is not Bantu. Still, in Ikaan this does not apply as such. new_statements.rule_in_words: Ikaan is described as a two-tone (H, L) language with downstep and a moraic TBU; the 375-page phonology thesis posits no word stress or accent, and its only reference to stress denies that tonal processes are attracted to any stressed/prominent position. No location of word stress is stated because none is described.
new_statements.exceptions: None; stress is simply not a parameter of the description. Prosodic prominence discussed only at sentence level (polar-question register expansion, breathy termination, final lengthening: Salffner 2010 sec. 5.4; Salffner 2017).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level phonology sketch (sec. 2.5.1) and tonal phonology; the p. 339 remark concerns word-internal and utterance-level tonal copying. Variety: Ikaan dialect of Ukaan (Ikakumo villages, Ondo/Edo States).
new_statements.identity_note: All Salffner sources describe the Ikaan lect of the Ukaan cluster (spoken in the two Ikakumo villages, Ondo and Edo States); the other lects (Ishe/Ise, Auga/Iigau, Ayanran/Iyinno) are not mutually intelligible with it in all cases and are covered only by inaccessible Nigerian theses and Jungraithmayr 1973 (Ishe). Glottolog treats these as dialects under ukaa1243; dialect-level glottocode for Ikaan not verified here.

new_statements.quote: The Ikaan tone system is a two-tone-plus-downstep system that shows automatic/non-automatic downstep patterns that are typologically very rare and are predicted by linguistic theory not to exist (cf. Salffner 2010b). Tone is active not only in the phonology and the lexicon, but also throughout the grammar in derivation, inflection, syntax, and semantics.

new_statements.relation_note: Wrong item, but the paper actually delivered (Salffner 2015, already checked held by the project) is about Ikaan and agrees with the catalog/existing statement: a two-tone-plus-downstep tone language with no stress statement. The listed 2013 paper remains not-opened; nothing new about stress is expected from it (its topic is final nasal vowels and consonants; Salffner 2015 p. 265 lists it as ELAR bundle ikaan563 and as SOAS Working Papers in Phonetics and Linguistics, ed. Connor Youngberg & Laura Kipp, pp. 311-332).
new_statements.rule_in_words: The paper that the open URL delivers is not the 2013 final-nasals working paper but Salffner's 2015 LD&C 'A Guide to the Ikaan Language and Culture Documentation' (SOAS Research Online lists eprint 20871 under that 2015 title, and the archived PDF header reads 'Vol. 9 (2015), pp. 237-267.. A Guide to the Ikaan Language and Culture Documentation'). That paper gives only a thumbnail grammar: Ikaan is a two-tone (H, L) plus downstep language with tone active throughout the grammar; it says nothing about word stress, accent or prominence (the only hit for 'prominent' is 'play a prominent role during weddings'). The 2013 final-nasals paper itself was not opened: web.archive.org's CDX API refused connections twice, eprints.soas.ac.uk has no DNS by automated download, and the old SOAS working-papers page (volume-16) returns 404.
new_statements.identity_note: All Salffner works describe the Ikaan lect of the Ukaan cluster as spoken in Ikakumo (Ondo State, Nigeria); the catalog entry is 'Ikaan'. Blench 2005 (held by the project) treats the Ukaan cluster more broadly but has no stress or tone statement.
